title: Power law in doctoral supervision
question: Per degree k in Wikidata's P184 network: is log₁₀ CCDF a straight line in log₁₀ k for students per advisor above the KS-chosen x_min, and a straight line in k for advisors per student?

issues.text: Wikidata's P184 statements are a proxy for real supervisions: famous and well-documented academics and bulk-imported lineages are over-represented.
issues.fix: Read α as a property of the recorded network; check the tail's advisors (top chart) for imports.

issues.text: A heavy tail is consistent with cumulative advantage (preferential attachment) but doesn't prove it: long careers and big labs also give many students.
issues.fix: Claim only the shape; a growth model needs dated edges (students' doctoral years).

issues.text: The tail above x_min = 27 has 1,158 advisors and 68 distinct degrees: too few to tell a power law from an exponential or a lognormal.
issues.fix: Report the likelihood-ratio z and its 'can't tell' verdict, not just α.

alternatives.question: Does the MLE α stay constant as x_min rises from 10 to 40 (as a pure power law requires)?
alternatives.why: Drills into the tail's shape with the x_min scan on the board.

alternatives.question: Is the tail of students per advisor heavier for mathematicians (P101) than for chemists?
alternatives.why: Drills into fields; needs the advisors' fields of work.

alternatives.question: Do advisors who already had students in a decade get more in the next (preferential attachment)?
alternatives.why: Expands to dated edges to test the mechanism, not only the shape.

hypotheses.statement: Above x_min, the log share of advisors with at least k students falls linearly in log k (a power law, slope 1 − α ≈ −3).
hypotheses.null: The log CCDF bends in log k (lognormal, cutoff): its slope is not constant.

outcome.concept: Share of advisors with at least k students

hypotheses.statement: The log share of students with at least k advisors falls linearly in k (exponential: each extra advisor is several times rarer).
hypotheses.null: It falls linearly in log k instead (heavy-tailed).

outcome.concept: Share of students with at least k advisors

concepts.label: Doctoral advisor
concepts.description: A person with one or more P184 statements pointing at them.
concepts.why: The node whose out-degree is studied.

concepts.label: Degree
concepts.description: k: students per advisor or advisors per student.

concepts.label: CCDF
concepts.description: P(K ≥ k), the share with k or more.
concepts.why: The outcome; on log-log axes a power law is a straight line.

concepts.label: Network direction
concepts.description: students per advisor (out-degree) or advisors per student (in-degree).

concepts.label: Power-law exponent
concepts.description: α by maximum likelihood for a given x_min.
concepts.why: The size of the effect; compare with the regression slope.

strategy.detail: α = 1 + n_tail / Σ n ln(k/(x_min − ½)) over k ≥ x_min (step xmin_scan)

concepts.label: Doctoral year
concepts.why: Needed to test preferential attachment as a growth process.

strategy.detail: Wikidata P69 (educated at) with qualifier P582/P585, or the Mathematics Genealogy Project, matched on the student's QID

data.request: For each P184 edge, the year the student's doctorate was awarded
data.source: Wikidata (P69 qualifiers, P1026 academic thesis), Mathematics Genealogy Project
data.why: To see whether advisors with more students gain students faster.

method.summary: A straight line of log₁₀ CCDF on log₁₀ k (H1, degrees k ≥ x_min) and on k (H2) with weak priors; the slope's posterior and the residuals' curvature decide. A regression on a CCDF has correlated residuals, so its interval is too narrow: the MLE and the likelihood-ratio test (steps xmin_scan, compare) are the real estimates.

steps.title: Degree histograms from Wikidata
steps.detail: Two SPARQL GROUP BY counts over P184: students per advisor (out_hist) and advisors per student (in_hist).

steps.title: CCDF per degree
steps.detail: ccdf = cumulative sum of n from the top / total; log_k, log_ccdf (steps out_deg, in_deg, curves).

steps.title: Scan x_min
steps.detail: MLE α and KS distance for x_min = 1…40; the smallest KS picks the tail (xmin_scan, best).

steps.title: Regress and compare
steps.detail: Regression of log_ccdf on log_k (network = students per advisor, k ≥ x_min) and on k (advisors per student); Vuong's test in compare.

steps.title: Power law, exponential, or can't tell
steps.detail: Use compare.verdict (|z| > 2) with the slopes; report 'heavy-tailed' when the power law beats the thin-tailed model on the whole range but not in the tail.

caveats: Wikidata coverage: recorded supervisions, not all supervisions; bulk imports inflate some advisors.
Rows of a CCDF are cumulative, so a regression on them overstates certainty; prefer the MLE and likelihood ratio.
The discrete MLE uses the continuous approximation with a ½ offset, accurate for x_min of about 6 and up.
Power law, lognormal and stretched exponential are hard to tell apart with ~1,000 tail values; the lognormal is not fitted here.
